record.paper_title: On some open problems of number theory
record.original_question: Are there infinitely many twin-prime pairs, meaning pairs of primes p and q with q - p = 2?

artifact.self_contained_problem: A twin-prime pair is an ordered pair $(p, q)$ of prime numbers satisfying $q - p = 2$ (equivalently, both $p$ and $p+2$ are prime). Examples include $(3,5)$, $(5,7)$, $(11,13)$, $(17,19)$, $(29,31)$. Prove or disprove: there exist infinitely many twin-prime pairs.
artifact.status_search_result: The twin prime conjecture remains a famous open problem in number theory. The best known partial results stem from work of Zhang (2013), Maynard, and the Polymath project, which established that there are infinitely many pairs of primes differing by at most some bounded constant (currently 246 unconditionally), but the bound of 2 has not been achieved.

status_evidence.title: Twin prime - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: The twin prime conjecture states that there are infinitely many twin primes; this is one of the great unsolved problems of number theory.
status_evidence.claim: The twin prime conjecture is still open.

status_evidence.title: Bounded gaps between primes - Polymath
status_evidence.snippet: Establishing that there are infinitely many pairs of primes differing by at most 246.
status_evidence.claim: Best known unconditional bound on prime gaps is 246, not 2.
